description: Amazon purchase histories mix recurring preferences with changes in buying intent, and their sparse observations make large attention models prone to overfitting. The previous attempts test masked Transformers, causal Transformers with taste features, and candidate-conditioned item similarity; this experiment instead tests a recurrent state model. A GRU learns how each purchase updates the user's state, sharing the same update rule across history lengths. This provides a different hypothesis: learning how interests evolve can outperform reconstructing purchases or matching individual historical items. Training uses BPR-max, which emphasizes difficult sampled negatives and directly learns relative rankings. Each category has one jointly trained network and one selected checkpoint, with no independent auxiliary predictor. Validation ranks the actual held-out purchase against 99 unique negatives for 200 users using evaluation seed 42 and reports macro-average HR@10. A host validation score above 0.505 would support this hypothesis; a weaker result would suggest that recurrent compression loses useful history information. The script preserves the supplied splits and writes the matching routed predictor for the host's independent evaluation; it does not access test files or fabricate a submission.
method: Trains one independent network per category using seed 42: a two-layer, 128-dimensional GRU over up to 64 purchases, with shared input/output item embeddings, dropout, LayerNorm, a linear output projection, and jointly learned item biases. BPR-max training uses 256 shared sampled negatives, masks purchases in the training window, and adds a negative-score penalty. AdamW, gradient clipping, validation-based learning-rate reduction, and early stopping control optimization. Each category retains one validation-selected checkpoint. The generated predictor embeds the matching architecture, routes by dataset name, and scores candidates from the last nonpadding recurrent state. Supplied splits remain unchanged; no ensembles or separately fitted auxiliary scorers are used.

method: Trains one independent bidirectional Transformer per category: 96-dimensional embeddings, two attention blocks, two heads, length-64 histories, and 0.25 dropout. description: Tier 2: add learned relative-position attention biases to the existing masked-history transformer. Absolute positions identify sequence slots, but they do not directly express how far an interaction lies from the prediction position. This can make learning recency and short-range dependencies unnecessarily difficult, especially across histories of different lengths. Each attention head will learn a signed distance bias, allowing it to distinguish recent interactions from older context. The biases start at zero, so training begins with the previous attention behavior. This is one controlled architectural change; masking, scoring, loss, and training defaults remain unchanged. All added parameters are trained jointly inside the category network, with exactly one selected checkpoint per category. Validation and the generated predictor use the same architecture and inference processing; the host remains responsible for held-out evaluation.

The architectural change adds jointly learned, zero-initialized per-head signed relative-distance attention biases, clipped at ±32. Training masks the final item plus 15% of interior items and uses sampled softmax with 512 uniform negatives, normalized tied item embeddings, learned item biases and score scale, and AdamW.
